title: Thinking: Heuristics and Biases
summary: Availability Heuristic, Anchoring Heuristic, Representativeness Heuristic, Simulation Heuristic, Peak-End Rule, Base Rate Fallacy, Framing Effect, Scarcity Principle, Contagion Heuristic, Satisficing, Elimination Heuristic, Lexicographic Heuristic.
objectives: Describe simulation, peak-end, base rate, framing heuristics.
Explain scarcity, contagion, satisficing, elimination, lexicographic heuristics.
revision: Heuristics: Availability (ease of recall), Anchoring (first info), Representativeness (prototype similarity), Simulation (imaginability), Peak-End (peak and end moments), Base Rate (prior probability), Framing (presentation), Scarcity (limited opportunity), Contagion (contact avoidance), Satisficing (good enough), Elimination (remove options), Lexicographic (best on key attribute).
traps: Availability = ease of recall, not actual frequency.
confusions: Confusing anchoring (first information) with availability (ease of recall).
Believing heuristics always lead to errors.

notes.t: Availability Heuristic
Judging the frequency or probability of an event by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid or recent events are judged as more likely.
Anchoring Heuristic
Relying too heavily on the first piece of information (anchor) when making decisions, even when that anchor is irrelevant.
Representativeness Heuristic
Judging probability based on how similar something is to a prototype, ignoring base rates.
Simulation Heuristic
Judging the likelihood of an event based on how easily it can be imagined.
Peak-End Rule
People judge experiences largely based on how they felt at the peak and at the end, rather than the total sum or average.
Base Rate Fallacy
Ignoring base rate information (prior probability) in favor of specific information about a particular case.
Framing Effect
Decisions are influenced by how choices are presented (framed), even when the underlying options are identical.
Scarcity Principle
People value opportunities more when they are scarce or limited.
Contagion Heuristic
Avoiding objects or people that have been in contact with something considered contaminated or negative.
Satisficing
Choosing the first option that meets a minimum threshold rather than searching for the optimal option.
Elimination Heuristic
Eliminating options one by one based on criteria until one remains.
Lexicographic Heuristic
Ranking options by the most important attribute and choosing the best on that attribute alone.
UGC NET frequently asks about availability, anchoring, representativeness heuristics, and framing effect.
